lead: Coreference links two mentions that point to the same entity. Anaphora resolution finds the antecedent that an anaphor such as a pronoun depends on. The work matters for summarization, question answering, translation and chatbots that must track who did what. The chapter covers chains, Hobbs' algorithm, Centering Theory, mention-pair models, clustering, and precision, recall and F1. It also notes Indian-language zero pronouns.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.7 for discourse links, Chapter 4.6 for semantic roles, and Unit 3 for parse trees.

blocks.text: A mention is a span of text that refers to an entity: a name, a pronoun, a noun phrase, or a dropped element. An entity is the thing in the world being talked about. A coreference chain is the set of all mentions that point to one entity. In the figure, Ravi and He form one chain; Meera and She form a second; report and it form a third.

An anaphor is a mention whose meaning depends on another mention, its antecedent. 'He' is an anaphor, and 'Ravi' is its antecedent. In cataphora the antecedent comes later: in 'After she paid, Meera left', she points forward to Meera. An expletive it carries no referent: 'It is raining' has no antecedent for it.

Zero anaphora is a missing pronoun that the reader recovers from context or agreement. Hindi 'Ravi aaya aur ___ baith gaya' means 'Ravi came and sat'; the subject of sat is dropped. Indian languages use this often.
Hobbs' algorithm resolves a pronoun by searching the parse tree. It is syntactic and cheap, and it uses number, gender and person agreement.

items: Start at the pronoun node in the parse tree.
Climb to the first NP or S above it; call it X.

Search the branches below X to the left of the path from the pronoun, left-to-right, breadth-first, proposing NP nodes that agree in number, gender and person; never propose the pronoun's own NP. If X is an S node, also search the branches to the right of the path in the same way, stopping at any NP or S you meet.

If no antecedent is found and X is not the topmost S of the sentence, climb to the next NP or S and repeat, skipping branches already visited. If no antecedent is found and X is the topmost S of the sentence, repeat the whole search in the previous sentences, most recent first.
Stop at the first agreeing NP and return it as the antecedent.

blocks.text: Centering Theory adds discourse focus. Each utterance has a ranked list of discourse entities, the forward-looking centers C<sub>f</sub>, most salient first. The backward-looking center C<sub>b</sub> is the entity that links the current utterance to the previous one. Transition types describe how C<sub>b</sub> and the top-ranked C<sub>f</sub> move: Continue: C<sub>b</sub> stays and C<sub>b</sub> is the top-ranked C<sub>f</sub>. Retain: C<sub>b</sub> stays but is not the top-ranked C<sub>f</sub>. Smooth-shift: C<sub>b</sub> changes and becomes the top-ranked C<sub>f</sub>. Rough-shift: C<sub>b</sub> changes and is not the top-ranked C<sub>f</sub>. A pronoun normally points to C<sub>b</sub>, so centering constrains the search.

A mention-pair model scores a pair (mention m, candidate antecedent a) with features and keeps the best antecedent. An entity-based model scores adding m to a whole cluster. Features include number, gender and person agreement; distance in sentences; salience such as subject or first mention; syntactic role; string match; and semantic compatibility. WordNet sense compatibility can help, but sense is not coreference; see Chapter 4.5.

items: Clustering: link accepted pairs, then take transitive closure. Over-merging is a risk, so add cannot-link constraints.
Indian languages: dropped pronouns need a zero-pronoun step; rich verb agreement gives number, gender and person, which supplies the missing features.
Cross-lingual: English pronouns may vanish in Hindi or Tamil, and reappear in translation, so alignment must track entities, not words.

blocks.text: P = C ÷ N_pred, R = C ÷ N_gold, F1 = 2PR ÷ (P + R)
blocks.where: C is the number of correct links; N_pred is the number of predicted links; N_gold is the number of gold links; P is precision and R is recall.

blocks.text: Evaluation: precision P = correct links ÷ predicted links. Recall R = correct links ÷ gold links. F1 balances them. Some metrics count links, as in MUC-style scoring; some score whole entities, as in CEAF; and some average per-mention scores, as in the CoNLL shared-task metric. Entity F1 and mention F1 are not interchangeable.

figure.caption: Each line joins the mentions of one entity, laid out in reading order. Notice that 'He' links back to Ravi, not to the nearer Meera.

spec.aria: A graph of three coreference chains in reading order: Ravi1, He and Ravi2 in one chain; Meera1, Meera2 and She in a second; report and it in a third.

examples.question: Resolve the pronouns in: 'Ravi met Meera at the cafe. He was carrying a red folder. Meera asked Ravi for the report. She read it quickly.' Give the coreference chains. Then a system predicts 3 coreference links, of which 2 are correct; the gold standard has 5 links. Compute precision, recall and F1.
steps: Mentions: Ravi₁ (sentence 1), Meera₁ (1), He (2), Meera₂ (3), Ravi₂ (3), report (3), She (4), it (4).
He agrees with Ravi: singular masculine. Chain 1 is (Ravi₁, He, Ravi₂).
She agrees with Meera: singular feminine. Chain 2 is (Meera₁, Meera₂, She).
it refers to the report: neuter thing. Chain 3 is (report, it).
Predicted links = 3, correct links = 2, gold links = 5.
examples.answer: Chains are (Ravi₁, He, Ravi₂), (Meera₁, Meera₂, She), and (report, it); precision = 0.6667, recall = 0.4, F1 = 0.5.
examples.check:
predicted = 3
correct = 2
gold = 5
p = correct / predicted
r = correct / gold
f1 = 2 * p * r / (p + r)
print(f'{p:.4f}')
print(f'{r:.1f}')
print(f'{f1:.1f}')

traps: Anaphora is not coreference: an expletive it has no antecedent, and a bridging description can depend on discourse without sharing an entity.
Do not pick the nearest noun by default; agreement and discourse focus can point farther back.
Links are unordered pairs; define them before computing precision and recall. Entity F1 differs from mention F1.
Gender and number features can mislead with collective nouns, titles and names used for either gender.
Zero pronouns are not 'no referent'; in Hindi or Tamil the verb agreement may carry the missing features.

quiz.q: Define mention, entity and coreference chain.
quiz.a: A mention is a text span that refers; an entity is the thing referred to; a coreference chain is the set of mentions for one entity.

quiz.q: Why does expletive it in 'It is raining' have no antecedent?
quiz.a: It is a dummy subject. It fills the subject slot but does not refer to any entity, so no antecedent exists.

quiz.q: In 'After she paid, Meera left', name the anaphor, the antecedent and the type of reference.
quiz.a: Anaphor: she. Antecedent: Meera. Type: cataphora, because the antecedent comes later.

quiz.q: A system predicts 5 coreference links, of which 3 are correct. The gold standard has 4 links. Compute P, R and F1.

quiz.a: If some element of C<sub>f</sub> of the previous utterance is realized as a pronoun in the current utterance, then C<sub>b</sub> of the current utterance is also realized as a pronoun in it.

quiz.q: Why is a nearest-noun baseline wrong for pronoun resolution? Give one example.
quiz.a: The nearest noun may not agree or may not be the focused entity. In 'Ravi met Meera. He was carrying a folder', the nearest noun is Meera, but he must resolve to Ravi.

quiz.q: What is zero anaphora? Give an Indian-language example.
quiz.a: Zero anaphora is a dropped pronoun recovered from context or agreement. Hindi 'Ravi aaya aur ___ baith gaya' drops the subject of sat.

beyond: Not for the exam. Coreference is now a standard part of entity-centric NLP: it feeds knowledge-graph construction, long-document question answering and cross-lingual summarization. Research moves from mention ranking to end-to-end and multilingual models, including zero-pronoun languages. Search next for OntoNotes coreference, the CoNLL-2012 shared task, and multilingual coreference.
